extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, activists, campus administrators, policymakers, and legal researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedic overview of 'free speech zones' covering definitions, history, notable incidents and court decisions, criticisms, campus policies, and international examples related to designated protest areas and First Amendment/time-place-manner regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. court decisions stipulating that the government may reasonably regulate the time, place, and manner – but not content – of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the doctrinal basis for allowing restrictions such as designated protest areas; restrictions must be reasonable and are justified by considerations like crowd control and safety. Examples and cases throughout the article illustrate how courts apply this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: safety and crowd-control justification
rubrics_metrics.description: The stated purpose of free speech zones is to protect the safety of those attending the political gathering, or for the safety of the protesters themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities commonly invoke safety/security to justify designated zones at political gatherings, presidential appearances, and large events; critiques argue safety is sometimes a pretext for limiting visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: No content-based discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions may regulate time/place/manner but must not discriminate based on the content of the speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts lawsuits and ACLU challenges (e.g., ACORN v. Secret Service, Rank cases) alleging that authorities targeted anti-administration protesters while allowing supporters closer—illustrating that selective, content-based exclusion violates constitutional protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public forum doctrine (streets, parks, campus areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public streets and parks 'have immemorially been held in trust for the use of the public' and are traditional public forums; areas so classified cannot be treated as restricted to fewer speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hague v. CIO and later rulings establish that many campus spaces (parks, sidewalks) are public forums; a university cannot designate fewer areas than actually exist as public forums or regulate content in those forums (see Texas Tech decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Picketing and 'externalities' standard (less protection for conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Picketing and marching are afforded less protection than pure speech because of physical externalities they create, allowing regulation of demonstrations under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (Edwards v. South Carolina; Brown v. Louisiana; Cox v. Louisiana; Adderley v. Florida) show courts balance assembly rights against disruptive externalities when evaluating restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice and non-disruption requirement for campus events
rubrics_metrics.description: University rules commonly require advance notice to the university and require demonstrations to be held in locations that do not disrupt classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes campus policies originating in the Vietnam era and court decisions (e.g., Tinker; Texas Tech ruling) distinguishing public-school non-disruptive standards and indicating limits on private-university application of those standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility, placement and audience-reach as evaluative factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Designating protest zones 'out-of-sight' or 'out-of-earshot' reduces the ability of protests to reach audiences and affects participants' perceived efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics call such placements 'Orwellian' or 'protest pens'; research (Chamlee-Wright 2018 and other studies) is cited showing decreased visibility can depress willingness to participate and limit message transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-selective enforcement / equal treatment in policing protests
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement practices must not single out protesters based on viewpoint or selectively target opposition while tolerating supporters in closer proximity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include allegations that Secret Service-directed policing allowed pro-Bush signs nearer motorcades while moving anti-Bush demonstrators to remote zones; selective enforcement has been the focus of litigation and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret Service/security statutory authority and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal statute (e.g., §1752 and related provisions) makes it unlawful to willfully enter or remain in certain posted/cordoned/restricted areas around protected persons; the Secret Service asserts security considerations guide decisions about protester placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents use of that statutory authority and Secret Service practices (e.g., chain-link fenced zones at presidential events) but also shows courts and litigants challenging overbroad or discriminatory implementation—indicating the power is not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest in adequate capacity and proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Designated zones must be reasonably adequate to accommodate expected protesters; plans that hold only a small fraction of projected demonstrators are subject to criticism and legal challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Boston 2004 DNC controversy is cited where the proposed zone would have held as few as 400 of several thousand expected protesters—an example of a zoning decision criticized for being disproportionate to protest size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campus policy reform and statutory bans on 'free speech zones'
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative action in several states has outlawed public colleges and universities from establishing free speech zones (Virginia, Missouri, Arizona, Kentucky noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trend represents a legal/policy standard favoring campus-wide forums for expression rather than confined zones; the article cites state laws and institutional policy changes (e.g., Penn State, Tufts) as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative permitting, designation practices, and international variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Designated protest areas often involve permitting regimes and administrative decisions that vary by jurisdiction; in some countries protest parks/areas exist or applications are routinely denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include voluntary designated areas at Ottawa summit, designated Wan Chai areas in Hong Kong, Olympic protest parks in Beijing (whose permits were withdrawn/denied), Philippines 'freedom parks', and Singapore's Speakers' Corner—illustrating international diversity and human-rights concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance-planning tactics to minimize demonstrators (presidential advance manual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presidential advance manual advises organizers to prepare a site to minimize demonstrators (e.g., designate protest areas out of view, form 'rally squads' to shield press platforms, and remove demonstrators as a last resort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational guidance shows how event planning can be used to reduce protest visibility and is cited in the article as a controversial practice and evidence cited in litigation and criticism (ACLU discovery).
